name: Shanahan/Kubiak/McVay Wide-Zone Tree
description: The most widely copied offense in modern football. Built on outside/wide zone runs that stress defenses horizontally, with play-action and bootleg passing off identical run action, heavy pre-snap motion to diagnose coverage, condensed splits, and 11/21 personnel. Traces to Mike Shanahan's Denver staffs; Kyle Shanahan and Gary Kubiak carried it forward, and Sean McVay's branch (via Jon Gruden/Jay Gruden) converged on nearly the same principles independently.

name: Reid/Reich-Philadelphia West Coast Tree
description: Andy Reid's West Coast passing game -- timing-based short/intermediate routes, spread shotgun run-pass options, heavy formation disguise, and structured but explosive shot plays off run-action. The Philadelphia branch (Frank Reich's staffs, then Nick Sirianni and Shane Steichen) descends from Reid's Eagles years and shares the same passing-game DNA even as each coach added his own wrinkles.

name: Air Raid (Leach/Mumme) Tree
description: The Hal Mumme/Mike Leach spread-passing system: four- and five-receiver spread formations, tempo, and a small package of quick-timing route concepts (mesh, four verticals, Y-cross) run at high volume rather than a large playbook. Kliff Kingsbury, a Leach quarterback and disciple, brought a direct version of it to Arizona.

name: Payton Air-Coryell Vertical Tree
description: Sean Payton's system blends Air Coryell vertical route concepts (numbered routes stretching the field deep) with pistol/shotgun spread formations and situational, scripted play-calling. Emphasizes explosive pass plays and a physical run game to set up shot plays downfield.

name: Erhardt-Perkins/Belichick Multiple Tree
description: The Patriots' concept-based system (plays are named for route concepts, not individual receiver assignments, so the same call means the same thing from any formation/personnel). Built for weekly game-plan flexibility, heavy use of the TE/H-back, and disguised protections. Bill Belichick's staffs (Josh McDaniels, Brian Daboll) carried it to their own head-coaching jobs.

name: Ravens Pistol-RPO System
description: A run-first system built around a dual-threat quarterback: pistol/shotgun zone-read and RPOs, an unusually heavy run-play rate, and play-action off the threat of the QB run game. Distinctive enough, and consistent enough across coordinator changes (Greg Roman, then Todd Monken), that it is treated as its own family under John Harbaugh's program.

name: Arians "No Risk It, No Biscuit" Vertical Tree
description: Bruce Arians' downfield-first passing philosophy: aggressive shot plays on early downs, a preference for one-on-one matchups outside the numbers, and a willingness to live with turnovers in exchange for explosive plays.

name: Campbell Power-Gap Physical Run Tree
description: Detroit's identity under Dan Campbell: a gap/power/duo run scheme with pulling linemen and physical double teams (rather than the zone-run families above), paired with an aggressive 4th-down and red-zone philosophy that is itself part of the offensive identity.

name: Seattle/Bucs Quick-Game West Coast (Canales Branch)
description: Dave Canales' system, shaped by his years as a Seahawks and Buccaneers quarterbacks coach: a quick-timing West Coast passing game with under-center play-action and an emphasis on getting the ball out of the QB's hand fast on early downs.

name: Kellen Moore Tempo-Vertical Spread
description: Kellen Moore's system (built across Cowboys and Chargers coordinator stops): shotgun-spread formations, uptempo pacing, and a heavier vertical-passing shot-play rate than most modern spread systems.

name: Independent / Coordinator-Directed Offense
description: Free NFL data only identifies the head coach per team-season, not the offensive coordinator who often actually calls the plays. For head coaches whose own background and public reputation is not a well-documented offensive system (most are defensive-minded HCs), we don't guess at an uncredited coordinator's scheme lineage -- their team's offense is tracked here instead of forced into a tree it may not really belong to.

name: Fangio Match-Quarters Tree
description: Vic Fangio's two-high shell defense: predominantly split-safety zone coverage (quarters/pattern-match) that disguises pre-snap and simulates pressure with four-man rushes instead of heavy blitzing, trading big-play prevention for tougher-to-defend third-and-medium. The single most influential defensive coaching tree in the league over the last decade -- this family includes both direct staff disciples and coaches whose systems are publicly documented as closely modeled on Fangio's principles.

name: Seattle/Carroll Cover-3 Tree
description: Pete Carroll's single-high Cover 3 system, built on size and speed at cornerback and safety to defend deep thirds with fewer defenders in coverage, freeing up the box for physical run defense. The scheme behind Seattle's "Legion of Boom" era and carried forward by Carroll's own coordinators.

name: Tampa-2 (Kiffin/Dungy/Smith) Tree
description: The Tony Dungy/Monte Kiffin Cover 2 variant with a middle linebacker dropping deep into the middle third -- built to limit explosive plays and force offenses to sustain long drives underneath. Lovie Smith is a direct originator-generation member; Matt Eberflus (whose "H.I.T.S." principle traces to Kiffin/Rod Marinelli) is a documented modern disciple.
core_concepts: Limiting explosive plays over sustained drives

name: LeBeau/Blitzburgh 3-4 Zone-Blitz Tree
description: Dick LeBeau's Pittsburgh zone-blitz system: a 3-4 front that disguises which four (or five, or six) rushers are coming and drops unexpected defenders into coverage, generating pressure without pure man-beating one-on-ones. Mike Tomlin inherited and has maintained this identity in Pittsburgh for nearly two decades.

name: Parcells/Belichick Multiple-Pressure Tree
description: A base 3-4 that shifts fronts and coverages week to week specifically to attack that opponent's protection scheme, rather than running one static system. Emphasizes situational multiplicity over a single identity. Belichick's Patriots defenses and Todd Bowles' aggressive pressure packages both descend from the Parcells coaching lineage.

name: McDermott/Buffalo Pattern-Match Tree
description: Sean McDermott's two-high pattern-match defense (developed under Jim Johnson and Andy Reid's Philadelphia staffs), frequently compared to the Fangio family for its shared reliance on disguised coverage over heavy pressure, but tracked separately given McDermott's distinct coaching lineage.

name: Fangio-Adjacent Match-Quarters (Rams Branch)
description: Raheem Morris' modern defenses, shaped by his run as Los Angeles Rams DC (2021, 2022-23) alongside the Fangio-branch coaching staff there, blending his earlier Tampa-2/Monte Kiffin background with the match-quarters principles that staff ran.

name: Ravens Attacking-Pressure Tree (Martindale/Orr Lineage)
description: Baltimore's defensive identity under John Harbaugh has been one of the league's most consistently blitz-heavy, disguised-pressure systems for years, spanning multiple coordinators (Wink Martindale, then Mike Macdonald, then Zach Orr) without losing its attacking character -- distinct enough from the more conservative two-high Fangio family to track separately.

name: Attacking Multiple-Front Tree
description: A looser grouping for long-tenured defensive coordinators-turned-HCs whose systems are well documented as multiple/attacking fronts but don't trace to one of the more specific named trees above.

name: Independent / Coordinator-Directed Defense
description: The defensive-side counterpart to Independent Offense: head coaches whose own background and public reputation is not a well-documented defensive system (most are offensive-minded HCs) are tracked here rather than having their team's defense attributed to an uncredited, unverified coordinator.
